justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 33.9 is anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing price or level at the time of the forecast, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short windows and no major catalysts were imminent. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 34.1, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with modest momentum or slight bullish bias in the underlying trend. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 34.5 continues that gentle upward trajectory, incorporating a longer-run drift component while acknowledging that prices tend to revert toward a slowly rising fundamental anchor over medium-term horizons.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard scaling of uncertainty with time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 1.2 units, which is quite tight and consistent with low realized daily volatility. At one week, the interval widens to about 4.2 units, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty and the increased chance of a directional move developing. By one month, the interval expands to 8 units, capturing the full range of plausible scenarios over a longer window including macro data releases, sentiment shifts, and positioning changes that accumulate over weeks.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a strong economic data print, a policy announcement, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could push the level well above 38.5 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode, unexpected negative news, or a broader market dislocation could drive the outcome below 30.5. The one-day interval is most vulnerable to gap-risk events such as overnight announcements or geopolitical surprises that bypass normal intraday price discovery.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during stress periods — even the one-week interval could prove too narrow. Liquidity conditions matter as well; thin markets can amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest, and any structural break in the trend underlying my point estimates would invalidate the mild upward drift assumption embedded across all three horizons.
